title: No One Is Excused From This
author: The Daily Stoic
summary: This Daily Stoic meditation makes the case that serious reading is an obligation of anyone who leads, not a hobby for the bookish. It opens with two warrior readers, Scipio Aemilianus, who trained in philosophy as hard as he trained at arms, and General James Mattis, who carried Marcus Aurelius on deployment and insisted that no Marine is excused from studying. From there it frames reading as a kind of time travel and a shortcut, a way of borrowing wisdom that others earned through painful trial and error. The piece draws on Seneca's idea of annexing the knowledge of the past, and it treats refusing to read as a form of arrogance. It widens Mattis's rule to everyone, from leaders and citizens to parents, then distinguishes knowing how to read from being a great reader. The closing paragraphs promote the Read to Lead challenge, but the core argument is that study must be a constant practice.
points: Mattis argued that failing to learn from history is costlier for soldiers than for other leaders because the price of ignorance is paid in body bags.
The essay frames books as manuals for living written so that later readers can start further ahead.
It extends the military maxim beyond soldiers to any leader, citizen or parent who wants a measure of success.
It ends by separating the ability to read from the discipline of reading well, which it treats as a skill to be trained.
quotes: It might seem a bit out of character for a powerful general—a fierce warrior—to go everywhere with a book tucked under their arm.
In fact, he argued, it was even more important for soldiers to learn from the past than it was for other leaders, because the alternative was filling up body bags as they made unnecessary mistakes.
Who would be so arrogant as to think they don’t need to do that? Who would be so stupid as to want to learn by trial and error what they can learn from the trial and error of others?
Books are literally manuals for living. They contain the wisdom of the collective human experience.
No one—no Marine, no leader, no citizen, no parent, no one who wants any measure of success—is excused from studying. Not now. Not ever.
We must drink deeply from history, from philosophy, from the books of journalists and historians and geniuses. Study the cautionary tales and the screw-ups, read about failures and successes.
